boundaries.p: The hikers reached the lake at noon ______ they ate lunch on the rocks by the shore.
boundaries.e: Two complete sentences joined by “and” need a comma before “and.” A comma alone creates a comma splice.

boundaries.p: Our science class visited the planetarium ______ the students learned how to find the North Star.
boundaries.e: “Where the students learned...” is a dependent clause, so it attaches with a comma. A semicolon or period would leave a fragment.

boundaries.p: Before the concert began ______ the musicians tuned their instruments backstage.
boundaries.e: An introductory clause is followed by a comma. A semicolon or colon needs a complete sentence before it.

boundaries.p: The recipe calls for three ingredients ______ flour, butter, and sugar.
boundaries.e: A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence. A semicolon needs a full sentence after it, too.

boundaries.p: My sister plays the violin ______ my brother plays the drums.
boundaries.e: A semicolon can join two complete sentences. A comma alone makes a comma splice, and no punctuation makes a run-on.

boundaries.p: The library, which opened in 1925 ______ is the oldest building on campus.
boundaries.e: The extra information needs a closing comma to match the one after “library.”

boundaries.p: The storm knocked down several trees ______ workers cleared the road by morning.
boundaries.e: A comma plus “but” correctly joins two complete sentences. A comma alone is a splice.

boundaries.p: Sara packed a jacket ______ she expected cold weather in the mountains.
boundaries.e: “Because she expected...” is dependent, so it can’t stand after a period or semicolon. No punctuation is needed.

boundaries.p: Astronomer Vera Rubin measured how quickly stars orbit the centers of galaxies ______ her data revealed that the stars moved too fast to be held in place by visible matter alone, providing key evidence for dark matter.
boundaries.e: Both sides are complete sentences, so a semicolon works. A comma alone is a splice, and no punctuation is a run-on.

boundaries.p: The Inca built roads across the Andes without iron tools or wheeled vehicles ______ many of those roads, paved with fitted stone, are still walkable today.
boundaries.e: A comma before “and” joins two complete sentences. The other choices either splice or misplace the comma.

boundaries.p: Mae Jemison, the first Black woman to travel in space ______ also trained as a physician and worked in the Peace Corps before joining NASA.
boundaries.e: The appositive needs a closing comma to match the one after “Jemison.” The sentence’s verb is “trained.”

boundaries.p: Although octopuses are solitary animals for most of their lives ______ researchers have occasionally observed them gathering in dense groups near rich food sources.
boundaries.e: “Although...” is a dependent clause, so a comma connects it. A semicolon, period, or colon would leave it stranded as a fragment.

boundaries.p: The museum’s newest exhibit features works by three sculptors: Ruth Asawa, known for her looped wire forms ______ Isamu Noguchi, who designed gardens as well as sculptures; and Augusta Savage, a leader of the Harlem Renaissance.
boundaries.e: Items in this list contain internal commas, so semicolons separate them. The later items use a semicolon, and this one must match.

boundaries.p: Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air ______ whales can communicate across hundreds of miles of ocean.
boundaries.e: “So” here joins two complete sentences and needs a comma before it, not after it.

boundaries.p: Maria Tallchief became the first American prima ballerina of the New York City Ballet in 1947 ______ performance in The Firebird two years later made her internationally famous.
boundaries.e: Two complete sentences must be separated. A semicolon does this; a comma alone is a splice, and no punctuation is a run-on.

boundaries.p: The bridge’s designers tested a scale model in a wind tunnel ______ a step that revealed a dangerous vibration long before construction began.
boundaries.e: “A step that revealed...” is not a complete sentence; it renames the action before it, so it attaches with a comma.

boundaries.p: For centuries, sailors crossing the Pacific relied on stick charts, lattices of palm ribs and shells used by Marshall Islanders to represent how ocean swells bend around islands ______ these charts were memorized before departure and never carried on the voyage itself, which meant that a navigator’s most essential instrument was his own trained recall.
boundaries.e: The clause beginning “these charts were memorized” is a complete sentence, as is the first part. A semicolon separates them; a comma makes a splice, however long the sentences are.

boundaries.p: The novelist Toni Morrison, who worked for years as an editor at Random House while raising two children and writing in the early mornings ______ published her first book, The Bluest Eye, in 1970.
boundaries.e: The long “who” clause opened with a comma, so it must close with one. The verb “published” is far from its subject “Toni Morrison,” which hides the need.

boundaries.p: Marine geologist Marie Tharp spent years plotting depth measurements by hand ______ when her finished map of the Atlantic floor revealed a vast rift valley running along the mid-ocean ridge, it gave crucial support to the then-controversial theory of continental drift.
boundaries.e: Both sides are complete sentences; the “when” clause belongs to the second one. A semicolon marks that boundary.

boundaries.p: Some early photographers relied on the wet-plate process, which required coating a glass plate with chemicals, exposing it, and developing it before it dried ______ as a result, those working outdoors had to bring a portable darkroom with them.
boundaries.e: “As a result” begins a new independent clause. A semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.

boundaries.p: According to linguist Marina Ortiz, children who grow up hearing two languages do not simply learn each one more slowly ______ rather, they develop a distinct system in which the two languages interact from the very start.
boundaries.e: “Rather” is a transition beginning a new independent clause, so a semicolon is needed. A comma would create a splice.

boundaries.p: Before announcing its decision, the committee reviewed proposals from three cities: Lyon, France ______ Porto, Portugal; and Ghent, Belgium.
boundaries.e: Because each item contains a comma, semicolons must separate them. The next item already uses one.

boundaries.p: The chemist’s notebooks, long thought to have been destroyed in a laboratory fire ______ surfaced in 2009 at an estate sale in Ohio, where a graduate student recognized the handwriting.
boundaries.e: The interruption opened with a comma and must close with one. A dash would be a mismatched pair.

boundaries.p: Few visitors to the ruined abbey notice the shallow grooves worn into its stone steps ______ yet these marks, left by centuries of monks walking the same path to prayer, may be the most intimate trace of daily life at the site.
boundaries.e: “Yet” joins two complete sentences, so a comma goes before it. No punctuation makes a run-on, and a colon doesn’t fit before “yet.”

form_structure_sense.p: The pack of wolves ______ across the frozen river each winter to reach its feeding grounds.
form_structure_sense.e: The subject is “pack,” which is singular, so the verb is “travels.”

form_structure_sense.p: Each of the runners ______ a number pinned to the front of a shirt during the race.
form_structure_sense.e: “Each” is singular, so it takes “wears.” “Of the runners” doesn’t change the subject.

form_structure_sense.p: Last summer, Dana ______ to the coast with her family and collected shells on the beach.
form_structure_sense.e: “Last summer” sets the past tense, which also matches “collected.”

form_structure_sense.p: The students finished ______ projects a full week before the science fair.
form_structure_sense.e: The plural possessive “their” shows that the projects belong to the students.

form_structure_sense.p: The ______ collars were all a bright shade of red, which made them easy to spot in the park.
form_structure_sense.e: “All” the collars belong to more than one dog, so the plural possessive “dogs’” is needed.

form_structure_sense.p: My aunt, along with her two sons, ______ at the farmers’ market every Saturday.
form_structure_sense.e: The subject is “aunt.” “Along with her two sons” doesn’t make it plural.

form_structure_sense.p: The collection of essays, published shortly after the author’s death, ______ her experiences as a nurse during the war.
form_structure_sense.e: The subject is “collection,” not “essays,” so the verb is singular.

form_structure_sense.p: Hoping to reduce noise in the city’s busiest neighborhoods, ______
form_structure_sense.r: officials installed sound barriers along the main highway.
w: sound barriers were installed along the main highway by officials.
the main highway received new sound barriers from officials.
noise was reduced by sound barriers along the main highway.
form_structure_sense.e: The opening phrase describes who was hoping. That must come right after the comma, and only officials can hope.

form_structure_sense.p: Since it was founded in 1892, the Sierra Club ______ to protect wilderness areas across the United States.
form_structure_sense.e: “Since” plus a past date calls for the present perfect “has worked.”

form_structure_sense.p: The ancient Greek city of Athens is famous for ______ democracy, in which male citizens voted directly on laws.
form_structure_sense.e: “Athens” is a singular city, and possession needs “its,” not the contraction “it’s.”

form_structure_sense.p: Neither the mayor nor the council members ______ willing to comment on the proposed budget.
form_structure_sense.e: With “neither...nor,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject, “members,” which is plural.

form_structure_sense.p: Among the most popular exhibits at the science center ______ a working model of a Mars rover and a room that simulates an earthquake.
form_structure_sense.e: The sentence is inverted: the subject is the compound “a working model... and a room,” so the verb is plural.

form_structure_sense.p: The discovery of thousands of clay tablets at the site, many of them inscribed with records of grain shipments and tax payments, ______ historians a remarkably detailed view of daily administration in the ancient city.
form_structure_sense.e: The subject is “discovery,” not “tablets” or “payments.” The long phrases between hide the singular subject.

form_structure_sense.p: Having studied the migration routes of arctic terns for over a decade, ______
form_structure_sense.r: researcher Carsten Egevang found that the birds travel far longer distances than earlier estimates had suggested.
w: the distances traveled by the birds were found by researcher Carsten Egevang to be far longer than earlier estimates had suggested.
earlier estimates of the birds’ travel were shown by researcher Carsten Egevang to be far too low.
it was found by researcher Carsten Egevang that the birds travel far longer distances than earlier estimates had suggested.
form_structure_sense.e: The person who “studied” must follow the comma. Each wrong choice puts distances, estimates, or “it” in that position, which creates a dangling modifier.

form_structure_sense.p: The architect’s drawings, together with a set of letters she exchanged with the city’s planners, ______ that the original design for the plaza included a much larger fountain.
form_structure_sense.e: The subject is “drawings,” plural. “Together with a set of letters” is an add-on, and “planners” is not the subject.

form_structure_sense.p: By the time the expedition reached the coast in 1805, its members ______ more than two thousand miles on foot and by canoe.
form_structure_sense.e: “By the time” plus a past event calls for the past perfect: the travel happened before reaching the coast.

form_structure_sense.p: Scholars who have compared the two manuscripts agree that the poet Phillis Wheatley revised ______ early verses extensively, though they disagree about when those changes were made.
form_structure_sense.e: The verses belong to Phillis Wheatley, so the singular “her” is correct. “Their” would wrongly point to the scholars.

form_structure_sense.p: The survival of these fragile paper maps, most of which were folded into trunks and forgotten for generations, ______ largely a matter of luck.
form_structure_sense.e: The subject is “survival,” which is singular. “Maps” and “generations” sit between the subject and the verb to mislead you.
